slides.say: Six workers paint a hall in ten days, and all the workers work at the same rate. How many days would four workers need to paint the same hall?

slides: Now, this one is a bit different. Remember the ratio table? There, the two numbers grow together. Twice the vases, twice the roses. But here it's the opposite. If I bring more workers, the job gets done faster, so the number of days goes down. More workers, fewer days. So a normal ratio table won't work here.
So before I calculate anything, let's think. Will it take more days, or fewer? There are fewer workers now, so the job takes longer. So it has to be [excited] more than ten days.

slides.say: So what can I cross out? Six and two thirds, and eight. They're both less than ten, so number one and number four are out.

slides: Now here's the idea. Let's measure the whole job in worker-days. One worker-day is one worker working for one day.

slides.say: Six workers work for ten days. That's six times ten, so the job is sixty worker-days of work. It's like one worker working alone for sixty days. And it's the same hall, right? So the job is still sixty worker-days, no matter how many workers do it.
Now we split those sixty worker-days between four workers. How many days does each one work? Four times d has to give sixty. So d is equal to sixty over four. That's fifteen days.
So number three is our answer.
at: <d is equal to sixty over four

slides.say: And where do the other choices come from? Six and two thirds is what you get from a normal ratio table, as if fewer workers meant fewer days. And twelve just adds two days for the two missing workers. Neither one makes sense.

So here's the rule. When one number goes up and the other goes down, their product stays the same. Like workers and days, or speed and time. And later in the course, you'll see an even faster way to solve questions like this. It's called the V method. I'll see you in the next question.
